summary: Describes scenarios in 3GPP packet networks, that is GPRS, that call for IPv6 and IPv4 transition. It focuses on cases where the user equipment connects to nodes in other networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Mobile phone networks must move from the old internet addressing to the new one. This memo lists the situations where old and new have to work together.

questions: how does gprs support ipv4 and ipv6
what happens when ipv6 ue connects to ipv4 node
subtitle: Scenarios where mobile networks must support both IPv4 and IPv6 during transition.

tldr.problem: 3GPP mobile networks (GPRS, IMS) must support users and services that operate on either IPv4 or IPv6, but the transition from IPv4 to IPv6 creates mismatch scenarios where different endpoints speak different versions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs scenarios where a user equipment (mobile phone or device) connects through GPRS or IMS infrastructure to nodes or services that use a different IP version, or where the intermediate network uses a different version than either endpoint.
tldr.outcome: This document identifies and lists scenarios for future work to develop solutions. It does not propose solutions, just documents which mismatches are likely to occur during IPv6 deployment.

today: RFC 3574 is an Informational document describing scenarios identified during early IPv6 deployment in 3GPP networks. It lists problems for which solutions are documented separately. The document has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Scope and 3GPP Network Basics
sections.content:
This document describes transition scenarios in Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) packet networks during IPv6 deployment. The focus is on scenarios where User Equipment (UE)—a mobile phone or device—connects to nodes outside the GPRS network, such as services on the Internet.

The scope is limited to 3GPP Releases 1999, 4, and 5, and covers both GPRS (General Packet Radio Service) and IMS (IP Multimedia Core Network Subsystem). The document lists scenarios but does not propose solutions; further analysis may show some scenarios are not practically relevant.

A simplified GPRS architecture has the UE, the GGSN (Gateway GPRS Support Node) which anchors mobility and acts as the default router, and peer nodes in other networks. The UE activates a PDP (Packet Data Protocol) Context to the GGSN, which configures the UE's IP address and other settings. Three types of PDP Context exist: IPv4, IPv6, and PPP. A UE can have multiple simultaneous PDP Contexts.
sections.eli5: A mobile phone (UE) connects through the mobile network to the internet or other networks using a dedicated channel (PDP Context) that gets an IP address and other settings.

sections.title: IP Multimedia Subsystem Architecture
sections.content:
IMS is an architecture for multimedia services via SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) infrastructure, specified in 3GPP Release 5. It comprises SIP proxies, servers, registrars, and Media Gateways that connect to non-IP networks like the PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network).

The key SIP components are the P-CSCF (Proxy-Call Session Control Function, the first IMS contact point), the I-CSCF (Interrogating-CSCF, the contact point for connections to a subscriber), and the S-CSCF (Serving-CSCF, which performs session control and acts as a SIP Registrar).

Critically, the IMS is exclusively IPv6. IMS-capable UEs must activate an IPv6 PDP Context to use IMS. All traffic to IMS is IPv6, including both signaling and user data, even if the UE is dual-stack capable. This does not prevent the UE from using other unrelated services (such as corporate access) on IPv4.
sections.eli5: IMS is the phone call system built on the new internet addresses. It only speaks IPv6, so phones that want to use it must activate a special connection that gives them an IPv6 address.

sections.title: GPRS Transition Scenarios
sections.content:
When GPRS UEs contact services outside the GPRS network, five scenarios arise:

Dual Stack UE: A dual-stack capable UE with simultaneous IPv4 and IPv6 PDP Contexts can connect to both IPv4 and IPv6 nodes. However, IPv4 addresses may be scarce, so operators might allocate private IPv4 addresses or require the UE to activate IPv4 only when needed.

IPv6 UE over IPv4 network: An IPv6-capable UE and GGSN in the GPRS network may need to reach an IPv6 peer node through an IPv4-only intermediate network. A tunneling or translation mechanism is needed.

IPv4 UE over IPv6 network: A legacy IPv4-only UE must reach an IPv4 peer through an IPv6 GPRS operator network. This requires the operator to provide an IPv4-capable GGSN with connectivity to the IPv4 Internet through the IPv6 network.

IPv6 UE to IPv4 node: An IPv6 UE tries to contact an IPv4 node in the legacy Internet. Requires a mechanism to bridge IPv6 to IPv4.

IPv4 UE to IPv6 node: A legacy IPv4 UE tries to reach an IPv6 node in the IPv6 Internet. Requires a mechanism to bridge IPv4 to IPv6.
sections.eli5: Five situations arise: both work (dual stack), old talking through new, new talking through old, new to old, or old to new. Each needs different help to make it work.

sections.title: IMS Transition Scenarios
sections.content:
Because IMS is exclusively IPv6, the number of transition scenarios is greatly reduced. Two main scenarios arise:

IMS UE to IPv4 node: An IMS UE (IPv6) wants to connect to a node in the IPv4 Internet through the IMS infrastructure, or vice versa. This occurs when the other node is outside 3GPP (such as a fixed PC with only IPv4). A mechanism must bridge IPv6 IMS to IPv4.

Two IMS islands over IPv4 network: In early IMS deployment, two separate IMS networks might only be connected via an IPv4 network such as the legacy Internet. A mechanism must allow two IPv6 IMS islands to communicate through IPv4.
sections.eli5: Because IMS only speaks IPv6, there are only two main problems: IPv6 IMS talking to an IPv4 node or service, or two IPv6 IMS networks connected only by an IPv4 network.
